guide.title: Frequently asked questions
guide.subtitle: Ten steps from a blank page to an exported mind map.
guide.steps.0.title: 1. Start with your central idea
guide.steps.0.body: Open the editor and type your topic on the first line. This becomes the root node of your map — the centre that every branch connects back to.
guide.steps.1.title: 2. Indent to create branches
guide.steps.1.body: Press Tab at the start of a line to indent it one level deeper, turning it into a child node. Press Shift+Tab to outdent and move it back up a level. Each level of indentation becomes a new layer in the map.
guide.steps.2.title: 3. Add siblings with Enter
guide.steps.2.body: Press Enter to start a new line at the same indentation level as the one above it, creating a sibling node. This is the fastest way to list several related points under one branch.
guide.steps.3.title: 4. Reorder nodes without retyping
guide.steps.3.body: Use Alt (Option on macOS) + Up or Down arrow to move the current line — and everything nested beneath it — up or down among its siblings, without cutting and pasting text.
guide.steps.4.title: 5. Enrich a node with quick commands
guide.steps.4.body: Type your configured trigger key (`, @, #, or ~) at the start of a line to open the quick command menu. From there you can set the node's text or markdown, attach a URL, add a detail image, or apply a colour or tag — all without leaving the keyboard.
guide.steps.5.title: 6. Switch layouts to match your content
guide.steps.5.body: Use the layout switcher above the map to try balanced, star, left, right, or tree diagram arrangements. A wide list of parallel ideas often reads better as a tree; a single central concept usually suits a balanced or star layout.
guide.steps.6.title: 7. Fine-tune the visual structure
guide.steps.6.body: Drag any node to reposition it, click a node once to adjust its text or background colour, or double-click to open its full detail panel and add notes, a title, a URL, or tags. Use the collapse (>) control on a node to tidy away a large subtree while you focus elsewhere.
guide.steps.7.title: 8. Zoom, centre and organise your workspace
guide.steps.7.body: Use the scroll wheel or the +/- controls to zoom, and the centre button to snap back to the middle of your map. Add more diagrams as tabs at the top of the editor panel, and double-click a tab to rename it.
guide.steps.8.title: 9. Export when you're ready
guide.steps.8.body: Use the export button in the top navigation bar to save your finished map as a PNG, WebP, or PDF image, or export the underlying outline as plain text.
guide.steps.9.title: 10. Back up with Google Drive (optional)
guide.steps.9.body: Open the Google Drive sync menu next to the theme toggle and sign in to push a copy of your workspace to your own Drive storage. Pull it back down on another device, or turn on auto sync so backups happen on their own while you keep working.
guide.sections.0.heading: Why write before you draw
guide.sections.0.body.0: Most mind mapping tools start you on a blank canvas: you place a shape, connect it, place another, and repeat. That's fine for a finished diagram, but it's slow for the messy, fast-moving part of thinking — the part where ideas are still being sorted.
guide.sections.0.body.1: Writing an outline lets you capture ideas at the speed of typing. Structure — what belongs under what — is expressed with a single keypress (Tab), not a drag-and-drop connection. The visual map becomes a by-product of organising your thoughts, rather than a separate task on top of it.
guide.sections.1.heading: Keyboard-first, mouse-optional
guide.sections.1.body.0: Every core action in the editor — creating a node, nesting it, reordering it, tagging it — has a keyboard shortcut. That matters most when you're brainstorming: switching to the mouse to draw a connector breaks your train of thought in a way that pressing Tab does not.
guide.sections.1.body.1: The mouse is still useful for the parts that benefit from direct manipulation: dragging a node to a new position, resizing the view, or picking a colour from a palette. The editor and the map stay in sync regardless of which one you use at any given moment.
guide.sections.2.heading: Local by default, backed up if you want
guide.sections.2.body.0: Everything you write is stored locally in your browser first — there's no server round-trip while you work, and no account is required to get started. That makes the tool suitable for early-stage notes, private planning, or anything you'd rather keep on your own device.
guide.sections.2.body.1: When you do want a backup or need to pick up a map on another device, sign in with Google through the sync menu next to the theme toggle. Push sends the current workspace to a private folder in your own Google Drive; pull brings the latest saved copy back down. Turning on auto sync repeats a push periodically in the background, so you don't have to remember to do it manually.
guide.sections.2.body.2: Exporting still works the same way it always has — to an image for sharing, or to text or JSON as a portable copy — so Drive sync is an addition to that workflow, not a replacement for it.
guide.items.0.question: What's the difference between Tab and Enter?
guide.items.0.answer: Enter creates a new node at the same level as the current one (a sibling). Tab indents the current line to become a child of the node above it. Shift+Tab does the reverse, moving a node back up a level.
guide.items.1.question: Can I change the trigger key for quick commands?
guide.items.1.answer: Yes. The trigger key that opens the quick command menu is configurable, with a choice of `, @, #, or ~, so you can pick one that doesn't collide with the characters you normally type.
guide.items.2.question: Do I need to plan the whole structure before I start?
guide.items.2.answer: No. Because reordering nodes is a keyboard shortcut away (Alt/Option + Up or Down) and indentation is a single Tab press, it's usually faster to write ideas roughly as they occur to you and reorganise afterwards than to plan the full hierarchy up front.
guide.items.3.question: What can I attach to a single node?
guide.items.3.answer: A node can carry a title, a URL, notes in plain text or markdown, tags, a custom colour, and a detail image. Double-click any node to open its detail panel and edit these.
guide.items.4.question: How do I share a finished map?
guide.items.4.answer: Use the export option in the top navigation bar to save the current view as a PNG, WebP, or PDF image, or export the outline as plain text if you want to share or reuse the underlying structure.
guide.items.5.question: How do I keep a map in sync across devices?
guide.items.5.answer: Sign in with Google through the sync menu next to the theme toggle, then use Push to back up your workspace and Pull to restore it on another device. Auto sync can push changes periodically without needing to trigger it manually each time.

templates.title: Frequently asked questions
templates.items.0.question: How do I use one of these templates?
templates.items.0.answer: Copy the outline text for a template, open the editor, and paste it in. Each line becomes a node and the indentation becomes the map's hierarchy automatically.
templates.items.1.question: Can I mix parts of different templates?
templates.items.1.answer: Yes. Paste in one template, then copy branches from another and paste them under the node where they belong — indentation is all that determines hierarchy, so pieces combine cleanly.
templates.items.2.question: Do templates support colours, tags or images?
templates.items.2.answer: Templates are plain text to keep them easy to copy and adapt. Once pasted in, use the quick command menu or a node's detail panel to add colours, tags, URLs or images to any node.
use-cases.groups.0.summary: Turning linear notes into a structure that's easier to review and compare at a glance.
use-cases.groups.0.scenarios.0.title: Lecture and reading notes
use-cases.groups.0.scenarios.0.body: Take notes as an outline during a lecture or while reading, then let the indentation become the map's hierarchy — main topic, sub-topics, supporting detail.
use-cases.groups.0.scenarios.1.title: Essay and assignment planning
use-cases.groups.0.scenarios.1.body: Draft an argument as nested points — thesis, supporting arguments, evidence, counter-points — and rearrange them until the structure holds together before you start writing prose.
use-cases.groups.0.scenarios.2.title: Exam revision
use-cases.groups.0.scenarios.2.body: Condense a topic into a single map that shows how sub-topics relate, making it easier to spot gaps than scrolling through pages of notes.
use-cases.groups.1.summary: Getting a shared, visual view of scope, structure, and open questions without a heavyweight planning tool.
use-cases.groups.1.scenarios.0.title: Project scoping
use-cases.groups.1.scenarios.0.body: List requirements as nested bullet points, group them by theme through indentation, and export the result as a reference during kickoff discussions.
use-cases.groups.1.scenarios.1.title: Roadmap and feature breakdown
use-cases.groups.1.scenarios.1.body: Break a feature area into smaller, more concrete pieces of work as child nodes, then reorder priorities with Alt + Up/Down as scope changes.
use-cases.groups.1.scenarios.2.title: Meeting and decision notes
use-cases.groups.1.scenarios.2.body: Capture discussion points live as an outline, then tidy the structure afterwards into a map worth referring back to.
use-cases.groups.2.summary: Getting ideas down quickly, without the friction of placing and connecting shapes on a canvas.
use-cases.groups.2.scenarios.0.title: Open-ended brainstorms
use-cases.groups.2.scenarios.0.body: Type ideas as fast as they come, using Enter for new ideas and Tab to nest related ones — sorting can happen afterwards, not while you're still generating ideas.
use-cases.groups.2.scenarios.1.title: Naming and concept exploration
use-cases.groups.2.scenarios.1.body: List variations under a shared root, tag the strongest candidates with the quick command menu, and colour-code by theme to compare options visually.
use-cases.groups.3.summary: Mapping structure that already exists — in a codebase, a content plan, or a knowledge base — so it's easier to reason about.
use-cases.groups.3.scenarios.0.title: System and flow diagrams
use-cases.groups.3.scenarios.0.body: Represent code structures, API endpoints, or user journeys as nested nodes, and switch to a tree layout when the content is naturally hierarchical.
use-cases.groups.3.scenarios.1.title: Content and documentation planning
use-cases.groups.3.scenarios.1.body: Outline pillars, sub-pages, and supporting notes for a piece of content or a documentation set, attaching reference URLs directly to the relevant node.
use-cases.groups.3.scenarios.2.title: Knowledge bases and reference maps
use-cases.groups.3.scenarios.2.body: Organise concepts, related decisions, and cross-references as a single visual map that's faster to scan than a folder of documents.
use-cases.groups.4.summary: Picking up the same map on a different computer, or simply making sure a long-running project has a backup.
use-cases.groups.4.scenarios.0.title: Switching between work and home
use-cases.groups.4.scenarios.0.body: Push a workspace to Google Drive at the end of a session, then pull it down on another computer to carry on exactly where you left off.
use-cases.groups.4.scenarios.1.title: Long-running planning documents
use-cases.groups.4.scenarios.1.body: Turn on auto sync for maps you update regularly, so a recent backup always exists in your own Drive without having to remember to export one.
